name: Periodontal treatment
lead: Periodontal treatment is the set of professional and home-care measures used to manage periodontal (gum) disease, which ranges from gingivitis to periodontitis with bone loss and tooth loss. Options include home plaque control, professional root-surface instrumentation, surgery for advanced cases, local or systemic antibiotics, lifestyle changes and ongoing maintenance.[1]

Periodontitis is reported to be the main cause of adult tooth loss worldwide and has been studied for associations with diabetes and cardiovascular disease.[1][3] Some randomised trials have examined whether treating it changes systemic markers, with varying results across outcomes.[2][8]

paras: Encyclopedic sources list brushing at least twice and flossing daily, regular professional cleaning and non-surgical instrumentation below the gumline, surgery where non-surgical therapy is insufficient, local drug delivery such as tetracycline, and systemic antibiotics in some cases, for which evidence of added benefit is low-certainty. Smoking cessation and diet are also discussed.[1] A 2017 review asked how many options exist for one disease, comparing non-surgical and surgical approaches.[5]

An 11-year maintenance study examined how residual pockets influence progression of periodontitis and tooth loss.[4] An earlier five-year study of 100 patients with furcation involvement reported that further destruction in those areas could be arrested after treatment.[7]

Periodontitis is associated with raised inflammatory markers and with diabetes, with a two-way relationship described between the two; many other associations are not proven causal.[1][3] A randomised trial of 120 patients with severe periodontitis compared intensive treatment with community-based care and measured endothelial function and inflammatory markers.[2] A 12-month randomised trial studied systemic effects of periodontitis treatment in type 2 diabetes,[6] and another trial examined periodontal treatment and preterm birth.[9]

Randomised trials have tested periodontal treatment against vascular, diabetic and pregnancy outcomes.[2][6][9] A Cochrane review cited in encyclopedic sources found insufficient evidence that treatment lowers blood pressure.[1] Registered trials include studies of pocket depth change, treatment in diabetes, myocardial infarction and cerebrovascular function.[10][11][12][13] Outcome details beyond the abstracts are not summarised here.

timeline.event: A five-year evaluation of multirooted tooth treatment is published.[7]
A randomised trial of periodontal treatment and preterm birth is published.[9]
A trial of intensive periodontal treatment and endothelial function is published.[2]
A 12-month trial in type 2 diabetes is published.[6]

card.summary: The umbrella of professional and home care for gum disease, from deep cleaning to surgery and lifelong maintenance.
card.note: Systemic-health benefits of treatment are studied but mixed or unproven.

quick.overview:
Periodontal treatment covers everything dentists and periodontists do to control gum disease: cleaning below the gumline, surgery in advanced cases, adjunct antibiotics and regular maintenance visits.

It is relevant to appearance because periodontitis can cause receding gums, loose teeth and tooth loss.
quick.mechanism: Treatment aims to remove bacterial plaque and calculus, reduce pocket depth and inflammation, and keep plaque under control through home care and maintenance.
quick.risks: Surgery and instrumentation carry the usual procedural risks such as soreness and sensitivity. Evidence that treating gum disease improves other conditions such as blood pressure is described as insufficient in one Cochrane review.
